actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: Echeneis naucrates occurs worldwide in tropical and temperate seas except for the eastern Pacific. In the western Atlantic it is found from Massachusetts south along the U.S. to southern Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea and Trinidade Island (Collette 2002, Simon et al. 2013). In the eastern Atlantic it is known from the Azores south to St. Helena Islands and along West Africa to Namibia (Collette ECA FAO Guide in prep). It appears to occur as a Lessepsian migrant in the eastern Mediterranean Sea. In the Indo-Pacific it is known along East Africa, the Red Sea, Persian Gulf (J. Bishop and B. Collette pers. comm. 2013), India, Indonesia, the Philippines, Japan, Australia, and the Hawaiian Islands. Its depth range is 20-50 m (Sakaff and Esseen 1999), but generally follows the depths at which its host occurs.
documentation.population: This species is common and locally abundant in most parts of its range. It is the most abundant of the remoras in all warm waters (but not eastern Pacific) (Heemstra 1986).
documentation.habitats: Unlike most other remoras, Echeneis naucrates is often found free-swimming in shallow inshore waters. It is commonly seen near shore and around coral reefs.  It is frequently sighted without a host and will occasionally stray into estuaries. It attaches temporarily to a wide variety of hosts particularly sharks, but also including rays, jacks, parrotfishes, sea turtles and also ships, buoys, and even bathers. Maximum size is 90 cm (SL) (Collette 2002), but reported to 110 cm (TL) (Lieske and Myers 1994). The all-tackle gamefish record is 5.38 kg (IGFA 2012). Its diet consists of small fishes, its host's parasites, and scraps from its host's prey. Juveniles will occasionally clean fishes at reef cleaning stations (Sazima et al. 1999).
documentation.threats: There are no major threats known for this species. There are no indications at present time of regional declines from harvesting.
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures in place.
documentation.use_trade: Echeneis naucrates have been used in artisanal fisheries as an aid to line-fishing. A line is tied around the caudal peduncle of the sharksucker and then it is released in the water. Upon attaching to a host, the remora and its host are pulled in by the fisherman. Taken with drift nets and trawls. Occasionally marketed fresh (Collette 2002) and seen in a Dakar market and in the Philippines (B. Collette and J. Williams pers. comm. 2012).
documentation.rationale: Echeneis naucrates is widely distributed, common and abundant where it occurs in shallow inshore waters. There are no known major threats, therefore, it is listed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Taxonomic note: This species is difficult to distinguish from the closely related Echeneis neucratoides which occurs only in the western central Atlantic (O’Toole 2002)
